HPI: 24-year-old man with first occurrence of brief spinning spells; onset 3 days ago. Episodes last about 20 seconds, triggered by rolling right in bed or looking up. Keeping the head still stops symptoms; well between spells. Brief nausea during episodes. Describes spinning rather than faintness. Has avoided provoking movements. No previous similar episode.

Perspective: I think I might be having a stroke.

PMH: No stroke, migraine or cervical spine disease.

PSH: No surgeries or admissions.

Meds: No daily medicines or sedatives.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

FH: My mom is fifty-one and she has high blood pressure.; My dad is fifty-four and he has diabetes.; I have one sister and she's healthy.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: In the examined posterior fields, clear breath sounds bilaterally.
Neurologic: Face symmetric; speech clear; tongue midline.

Neurologic: Right Dix–Hallpike after suitability review elicits brief vertigo and transient upbeating torsional nystagmus after a short latency. Left Dix–Hallpike after suitability review does not elicit vertigo or nystagmus.
Osteopathic: C1 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.
Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Assess neurologic red flags and cervical suitability, then perform a trained positional assessment; discuss canalith repositioning by a trained clinician if findings support posterior-canal BPPV; educate on temporary fall/driving precautions while symptomatic and arrange reassessment within 1 month; seek urgent care for persistent vertigo with new focal deficits or inability to walk.

2. Escalate immediately for acute focal deficits, severe gait impairment or a concerning persistent syndrome; obtain stroke-team evaluation and appropriate imaging; educate the patient about urgent neurologic warning signs; do not use a normal basic examination or an untrained HINTS assessment to exclude stroke.

3. Clarify whether vertigo is continuous for days rather than brief triggered spells; assess hearing and neurologic findings and arrange clinician evaluation; explain why the current time course is less typical for neuritis. Arrange reassessment if symptoms become persistent, hearing changes develop, or function worsens; persistent symptoms warrant a focused hearing and vestibular evaluation after urgent central causes have been considered.
